title: Braddick links clearer capital supervision to a new forum for system-wide resilience
summary: Katharine Braddick told UK Finance that the Prudential Regulation Authority wanted boards to understand why supervisors had identified a risk, what would address it and when action was expected. Her argument concerns the cost of uncertainty. A bank that misreads qualitative feedback may add controls that do little to address the underlying concern, commit resources unnecessarily or delay taking responsibility. Investors can inherit the same misunderstanding because much of their information about UK supervision comes from the banks and insurers they follow. Greater predictability is meant to make supervisory judgements easier to act on. The speech announces no general reduction in capital requirements.

The PRA can examine board papers, governance arrangements, business plans and the details of balance sheets across competing firms. An individual board sees its own firm in similar depth, but has less information about how a supervisor reached a judgement or what drove a comparison with peers. The UK approach Braddick described relies on discussions to identify the most important risks and a remediation plan with senior ownership. The PRA already publishes its supervisory approach and annual priorities. A five-year strategy due the following year was intended to give firms a longer view. Braddick also committed to timelier explanations of supervisory actions and, where useful, more context about peer comparisons.

For bank capital planning, two issues illustrate the consequences. Braddick said Basel 3.1 was reducing the discretionary component of requirements, improving predictability. Separately, uncertainty about when a firm can draw on its buffers can complicate management decisions even when the headline capital requirement is known. She cited steps already taken, including for smaller firms, and said the PRA would consider where more clarity was possible. The speech contains no bank-specific capital figures, revised buffer thresholds or timetable for such measures. The PRA also planned more direct contact with investors, analysts and rating agencies to learn which aspects of the regime remained unclear.

Operational risk required a different form of cooperation. Shared technology providers, including providers outside the regulated sector, can expose several firms to the same disruption. Even a firm confident of its own recovery plan may need other institutions or infrastructure to function before it can resume a service. Braddick said supervisors would give operational and cyber resilience greater weight. She described a consultation with the FCA due the following day on how firms should demonstrate preparedness. The address invited industry input and did not establish final requirements. The existing Cross-Market Operational Resilience Group would continue to develop practical guidance and sector workplans.

A new Systemic Resilience Council, chaired by the Bank, was expected to hold its first meeting the following month. Authorities would meet chief executives of systemically important firms and infrastructure providers to choose shared priorities and agree responses. The intended first subjects included the implications of frontier AI and assurance that firms could recover after severe disruption. The important distinction for a creditor assessing operating risk is between evidence about one institution and evidence that a critical service can recover across institutions. Braddick described the governance she wanted for that work. The address supplies neither results of a recovery exercise nor quantified estimates of losses avoided.

questions.question: When would greater clarity about buffers change a bank’s capital planning?
questions.detail: Braddick says uncertainty about buffer use can affect management decisions, without specifying new thresholds or an amount of capital that could be distributed. Before changing a valuation or payout forecast, compare the PRA’s eventual guidance with the bank’s disclosed management range, stress assumptions and distribution policy. Ask which constraint would bind in the downturn scenario and whether a clearer explanation would actually change the board’s action.

questions.question: What evidence would show that a critical service could recover across several firms simultaneously?
questions.detail: The speech identifies dependencies on shared providers that a single firm’s assurance cannot resolve. That matters for an investor assessing whether apparently diversified financial exposures might incur losses together. The relevant next sources would be the Council’s agreed priorities and any published sector exercise findings. Look for evidence on how participants verify resumption of the service across firms, including dependencies beyond their own operating environments.

questions.question: Will clearer feedback reduce costly remediation while improving the control the supervisor actually wanted?
questions.detail: A board may spend heavily yet fail to address the original concern if it misunderstands supervisory feedback. Lower compliance spending alone would therefore be ambiguous. Compare published supervisory priorities, a firm’s disclosed remediation milestones and evidence that its board has validated the outcome. The change to look for is faster closure of the specific underlying issue, alongside a credible explanation of the risk that remains.

limitation: The 18 November speech sets out the speaker’s supervisory intentions. It gives no final consultation rules, individual institution requirements or results from the proposed Council.
